Recent histological studies of reproductive tracts from females captured in the waters off Svalbard have provided critical insights into the species' reproductive biology. At temperatures typical of their deep-sea habitat around 5 °C [T = 5 °C], the gestation period yields an age at birth of roughly 1,715 days [ab = roughly 1,715 days], a remarkably protracted developmental duration that underscores the slow pace of life in this polar-adapted elasmobranch. This extended intrauterine period, during which the aplacental viviparous embryo relies on yolk reserves, is among the longest recorded for any shark species and is consistent with the general pattern of delayed life-history events observed in cold-water chondrichthyans. The size of neonates, at 40 cm [Lb = 40 cm] from snout to tail tip, positions them as relatively large at birth compared to many other elasmobranchs, conferring a survival advantage in the resource-poor environment of the deep Arctic and sub-Arctic oceans.

Males of this species attain sexual maturity at a considerably smaller body size than females, a pattern common among viviparous sharks where larger maternal body size supports greater fecundity. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is thought to reflect the selective pressures associated with supporting a lengthy gestation and producing relatively large free-swimming pups. Growth trajectory analyses based on bomb radiocarbon dating of eye lens nuclei have revolutionized our understanding of this species' life history. This extreme lifespan is likely a consequence of the shark's remarkably low metabolic rate in the frigid, low-productivity waters where it resides, combined with negligible predation pressure once it reaches adult size.

Comparative physiological studies have examined the metabolic constraints that govern the Greenland shark's extreme longevity and delayed maturation. Research employing aerobic scope measurements and routine metabolic rate assays indicates that individuals of this species grow at an exceptionally slow pace, with females achieving their maximum total length of 550 cm only after many decades of sub-zero habitat temperatures. Collectively, the life-history data for Somniosus microcephalus paint a picture of an organism that has evolved an extremely conservative energy allocation strategy, prioritizing somatic longevity and gradual growth over rapid reproduction, an adaptation well-suited to the stable but resource-limited environment of the deep Arctic Ocean.
